cards.q: What is the OSI reference model?
cards.a: The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) reference model (ISO/IEC 7498) describes networking in seven layers, each with a distinct function. It provides a vocabulary for discussing protocols, troubleshooting (is it Layer 2 or Layer 3), and matching real protocols to functions.

cards.q: List the seven OSI layers from top to bottom and their PDU names.
cards.a: 7 Application (Data), 6 Presentation (Data), 5 Session (Data), 4 Transport (Segment), 3 Network (Packet), 2 Data Link (Frame), 1 Physical (Bits).

cards.q: What is the function of the Transport layer (L4)?
cards.a: End-to-end delivery, ports, and reliability. It performs segmentation, reliability (TCP), and port multiplexing, with error recovery via ACKs.

cards.q: What is the function of the Network layer (L3)?
cards.a: Logical addressing (IP), best-path selection (routing), and fragmentation. Real-world protocol is IP and devices are routers.

cards.q: What is the function of the Data Link layer (L2)?
cards.a: MAC addressing, framing, and media access, plus error detection via FCS. It has two sublayers: LLC and MAC.

cards.q: What is the function of the Physical layer (L1)?
cards.a: Transmitting bits on the wire using electrical, optical, or RF signals; also defines connectors and topology. Devices include hubs and transceivers.

cards.q: What is the function of the Application layer (L7)?
cards.a: Interfaces applications to network services such as DNS names, file transfer, and email. Examples include HTTP, DNS, FTP, SMTP, and DHCP.

cards.q: What is the function of the Presentation layer (L6)?
cards.a: Data formatting, character encoding, encryption, and compression. TLS is sometimes associated with this layer in OSI terms.

cards.q: What is the function of the Session layer (L5)?
cards.a: Establishes and tears down sessions, tracks connection state, and does checkpointing. Examples include NetBIOS and RPC.

cards.q: What are the two sublayers of the Data Link layer and their roles?
cards.a: LLC (Logical Link Control, 802.2) handles multiplexing of protocols via EtherType; the MAC sublayer handles media access (CSMA/CD history and backoff) and addressing.

cards.q: Give the mnemonic for remembering the OSI layers.
cards.a: Top-down: All People Seem To Need Data Processing. Bottom-up (L1 to L7): Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away.

cards.q: How does the OSI model help in troubleshooting networks?
cards.a: It enables layer-by-layer isolation: physical (link lights, errors) to data link (MAC, VLAN, STP) to network (IP route) to transport (ports) to application. For example, 'ping OK but telnet fails' suggests a Layer 4 ports or Layer 7 issue.

cards.q: What is the #1 OSI exam trap regarding PDUs?
cards.a: Confusing PDU names: segment is the Transport layer PDU, packet is the Network layer (IP) PDU, and frame is the Data Link (Ethernet) PDU. Remember which name belongs to which layer.

cards.q: Where does encryption live in the OSI model, and what is the TLS caveat?
cards.a: OSI-wise, encryption lives at Layer 6 Presentation, so TLS is approximately Layer 6. In practice TLS is often described as Layer 4 or Layer 7, and exams want you to know both viewpoints without mixing them up.

cards.q: Map these devices to their OSI layers: switch, router, hub, firewall.
cards.a: Switch = Layer 2, router = Layer 3, hub = Layer 1, firewall/load balancer = Layers 4-7.

cards.q: Map MAC, IP, and port to their OSI layers.
cards.a: MAC = Layer 2 (Data Link), IP = Layer 3 (Network), port = Layer 4 (Transport).

cards.q: What commands help isolate which OSI layer is at fault?
cards.a: ping verifies L1-L3 (ICMP is L3), telnet to a port checks L4 reachability, and curl verifies L7. On devices, show interfaces shows L1 health, show mac address-table shows L2, and show ip route shows L3.

cards.q: Where do NAT, ACLs, and firewalls sit relative to OSI layers?
cards.a: These functions sit at layer boundaries: NAT is L3/L4, ACLs are L3+L4, and firewalls operate at L4-L7.
